competitors.name: QR Code Generator (qr-code-generator.com), Egoditor, now part of Bitly
competitors.model: 'Free' static codes, but PNG/SVG/EPS download requires an account; dynamic codes on a 14-day trial then annual subscription. Reviewers report being billed $119.88, $129.47, $190 and 'almost 200 dollars' per year, and one cites '$119/year forever to keep those codes working'
competitors.note: The category's default search result and the reason this app exists. It is also the single most hated product we found in any of our 23 categories: 3.3/5 on Capterra from 35 reviews with customer service at 2.7, and 1.5/5 on SmartCustomer across 349 reviews with an 11% recommendation rate. The trial-to-annual conversion is the business model, not an accident, 'They disable it after the 7 days and then when you have it printed tells you have to activate by purchasing an annual subscription' (Jessica R, Capterra, 8 Nov 2024). Their weakness is not a feature we lack; it is that a large, angry, high-intent audience is actively searching for the opposite of them. Note the funnel: QRCode Monkey, the friendly free tool below, is the same company's top-of-funnel.

competitors.name: Bitly (the parent brand's own QR product)
competitors.model: Free $0 to 2 QR codes/month. Core $10/mo (charged $120/yr), 5 QR/mo. Growth $29/mo annual ($348) or $35 month-to-month, 10 QR/mo. Premium $199/mo annual ($2,388) or $300 month-to-month, 200 QR/mo. Enterprise custom. Figures read directly off bitly.com/pages/pricing
competitors.note: Read those numbers again: the free tier meters you at two QR codes a month, and ten codes a month costs $348 a year. A QR code is roughly 400 bytes of arithmetic that a phone can compute in under a millisecond; Bitly is charging for the redirect and the dashboard, not the code. That is the whole strategic gap. Their real strength is trust-by-brand, 'bit.ly' in a URL is recognised, and genuinely good link analytics for marketers. Their exposure: a person making one WiFi card for a guest room is not a marketer and should never have met a pricing table.

competitors.name: QRCode Monkey
competitors.model: Free, no signup, static only, PNG/SVG/PDF/EPS, commercial use allowed. Monetised by upselling 'QR Code Generator PRO' (the Bitly/Egoditor product above) throughout the page
competitors.note: The most credible free competitor and the honest benchmark for our feature list: 'All generated QR Codes are 100% free and can be used for whatever you want. This includes all commercial purposes,' and 'The created QR codes are static so the only limitation is that you can't edit the QR code again.' It gives away logo embedding, full colour/eye/dot customization, and four export formats including EPS, all things we do not have. Two soft spots. First, it is a lead magnet: the page is dense with trial CTAs for the PRO product that generated the Capterra reviews above, so the user who came here to escape subscriptions is being walked back toward one. Second, it is a server-side generator, your payload is posted to their API, which is exactly the claim we can make and they cannot.

competitors.name: QR TIGER
competitors.model: Free tier: unlimited static codes plus 3 dynamic codes capped at 500 scans each. Paid tiers widely listed at Regular ~$7/mo annual or $9.99 monthly, Advanced ~$16/mo annual or $26 monthly (this is the tier that unlocks unlimited dynamic), Premium ~$37/mo. Prices taken from secondary comparison sites, not their own checkout, see confidence
competitors.note: The most aggressive SEO player in the category; if you search almost any QR question you land on their blog. Strong at bulk generation, GS1 codes, and enterprise-flavoured features. Their free static offer is genuinely unlimited, which means 'free static QR codes' alone is not a differentiator, everyone says it. What they cannot say is that nothing leaves the device, and what they will not do is tell you plainly that the dynamic code you are about to print is a lease.

competitors.name: Uniqode (formerly Beaconstac)
competitors.model: Free plan with 'no limit on static QR code creation'; dynamic from around $9/month, a Core tier around $49/month, then Plus and Business+, annual billing only, 14-day trial. Their own pricing table renders via JavaScript and could not be read directly
competitors.note: The enterprise/retail end of the category, badge printing, digital business cards, franchise rollouts, and the publisher of the best technical content in the space (their QR sizing and troubleshooting guides are the ones everyone else paraphrases). That content is the tell: an enormous amount of the category's real pain is *printing* pain, and Uniqode monetises answering it. We can build the answers into the tool instead of writing blog posts about them. Their own survey figure, that 29% of consumers have hit a dead QR link, is vendor-sourced but points at the right wound.

competitors.name: Flowcode
competitors.model: Free, up to 2 Flowcodes, analytics for 500 scans, ad-free. Pro Plus $25/mo billed annually, 50 codes and landing pages, 6,000 scans, 3 seats. Growth $250/yr annual only, 150+ codes, 10,000 scans, CRM/API. Growth Plus and Enterprise custom. Figures from flowcode.com/pricing
competitors.note: The design-forward one, aimed at brands and events, with strong art direction and a genuinely attractive code aesthetic. Every code is a Flowcode, it routes through their domain, which is the point of the product and the thing that makes it useless for a permanent sign. Two free codes is not a product, it is a demo. Nothing here threatens a person making a WiFi card, but Flowcode is the reason the category's visual conventions are dark-mode-and-neon, which is worth knowing when we choose not to look like that.

competitors.name: Canva and Adobe Express QR tools
competitors.model: Canva: free tool inside the editor, requires a free Canva account; PNG download on Free, but SVG export and transparent-background PNG require Canva Pro. Adobe Express: free tool, static codes, Adobe sign-in for the editor
competitors.note: The largest-volume competitor by actual usage, because millions of people are already inside Canva making the flyer and the QR tool is one panel away. That workflow advantage is unbeatable and we should not try. The seam is specific and worth naming: Canva makes static codes only, and the vector file, the one a print shop asks for, is behind Pro. A person who has just been told their SVG needs an upgrade is one search away from us, and they arrive knowing exactly which file they want.

competitors.name: The OS and the browser, Chrome's 'Create QR Code for this page', iOS Passwords Wi-Fi QR, Android 10+ Share Wi-Fi
competitors.note: The competitor that quietly eats two of our five content types. Chrome (desktop, Android and iOS) will make a PNG QR of the current tab from the address-bar share menu or a right-click, 'current page only, plain black-and-white, no logo, no editing.' iOS 18's Passwords app shows a Wi-Fi network QR on screen via Show Network QR Code, and Android has shipped Share Wi-Fi by QR since Android 10. So: for 'share this page with the person next to me' and 'let my friend onto the wifi right now', the phone already wins. What neither does is give you a *file*, a vector you can hand a printer, a sheet you can print and laminate, a code for a network you are not currently connected to, or a code for a phone number, an email address, or arbitrary text. Our WiFi feature must be positioned as the printable framed card for the guest room, not as the live hand-the-phone-over gesture.

competitors.name: The free client-side clone swarm (OpenQR, TotallyFreeQR, UnlimitedQRCodes, QRWink, FreeQRCodeGenerator.com, qrgenerator.org, QR Planet, QRStuff, the-qrcode-generator.com)
competitors.model: Free, no account, monetisation usually unstated, ads, SEO affiliate revenue, or an upsell to a dynamic tier
competitors.note: Our actual competitive set and the reason positioning is hard, exactly as with pdf-tools. 'No sign-up, no expiry, no watermark' is now boilerplate: it is the literal page title of at least three of these sites. The claim costs nothing to make, so it no longer differentiates, several of these are AI-spun affiliate properties whose comparison blogs also dominate the search results for QR pricing. Some are real and good. The competitive move is therefore not to assert the promise louder but to make it *checkable in the interface*: show the exact bytes encoded, run entirely offline with the network unplugged, and be a real installable PWA. Proof beats claim.

complaints.complaint: The code dies after the trial, and you only find out once it is printed. 'They disable it after the 7 days and then when you have it printed tells you have to activate by purchasing an annual subscription (almost 200 dollars).' And: 'They say it's free to create a QR code then after you create it and have it printed on your items they tell you it expires.' And: 'If you print materials with the QR code on it, they will only tell you AFTER you've paid for the printed materials that your code... will expire.'
complaints.source: Capterra reviews of QR Code Generator, Jessica R, 1★, 8 Nov 2024; Nicole B, 1★, 4 Oct 2024. SmartCustomer review of qr-code-generator.com, Courtney G, 8 Dec 2024
complaints.weWinIf: The word 'static' is jargon; the promise is 'this code contains your data, so there is nothing left that can be switched off.' Prove it rather than assert it: print the exact encoded string underneath the preview, character for character, with a byte count. When someone sees `WIFI:T:WPA;S:Nest;P:...;;` or their own `https://` URL sitting there in full, they can see there is no third-party domain in the loop. That single readout is the entire product argument, it is roughly twenty lines of code, and no competitor will copy it because for most of them it would expose their redirect host.

complaints.complaint: 'At no time during the purchase process did QR Code Generator PRO mention that their codes would expire at the end of a year unless we kept paying and paying... I would have to pay $119/year forever to keep those codes working.' A second reviewer: 'Free QR code will expire quickly if you dont pay huge annual fee!... $120 fee for 2 QR codes.'
complaints.source: Capterra, Rebecca K, 1★, 14 Apr 2025; Angie M, 1★, 2 Sep 2024
complaints.weWinIf: State the negative claim in plain words at the top, where a competitor puts its pricing table: there is no plan, no tier, no counter, and no renewal, because there is no server. Then put the arithmetic beside it, Bitly's free tier is 2 QR codes a month and ten a month is $348 a year, so the reader understands what they are being spared. Do not soften this into 'we respect your privacy.'

complaints.complaint: Annual charges dressed up as monthly ones. 'I selected a basic monthly plan $15.98, charge me for a year $190.' 'I was charged 129.47 for a full year' after believing the plan was $9.99/month. 'Charged for a subscription I never knew I had', $119.88, plus a prior $119.88 the year before. 'We paid for 2 years worth of this tool to use during 2 days' with the company refusing even a partial refund.
complaints.source: SmartCustomer reviews of qr-code-generator.com (1.5/5, 349 reviews, 11% would recommend), Alycia W, 29 Apr 2025; Garrison R, 5 May 2025; Marcus D, 16 May 2025. Capterra, Konstantin K, 1★, 21 Nov 2024
complaints.weWinIf: There is no payment surface anywhere in the UI: no card field, no trial, no 'upgrade', no plan comparison. The tip jar stays a text link in the header and the footer, never a filled button, never on the download path, and never worded as unlocking anything. Someone arriving straight from a $190 surprise charge should be able to confirm in three seconds that no charge is possible here.

complaints.complaint: 'They deleted my QR code and there is no way to retrieve it... No customer service. Unclear policies.' The dashboard that was supposed to be the benefit becomes the single point of failure, lose the account, lose the artwork.
complaints.weWinIf: Because our codes are permanent, the durable asset is the *file*, and the real-world failure is losing it, the menu gets reprinted in two years and nobody can find the original SVG. We currently persist nothing: reload the page and the work is gone (app.js keeps everything in the in-memory `fields` object). Add a device-local history of codes made, label, payload, error-correction level, date, with one-tap re-export of the identical file, plus an export/import of that list as JSON so it can be filed with the artwork. Nobody can delete it because nobody but the user has it.

complaints.complaint: The vector file, the one the print shop actually asks for, is the paywall. Canva makes QR codes free but 'SVG export and transparent background PNG require a Pro subscription'; qr-code-generator.com 'requires account signup to download in PNG, SVG, or EPS formats.'
complaints.source: Canva QR generator coverage and qr-code-generator.com's own free-QR-creator page, via SERP summaries
complaints.weWinIf: SVG is already free and first-class here (helpers.js `qrToSvg`, one path of module squares with `shape-rendering="crispEdges"`, genuinely correct output). We should say so where the competitor puts the upgrade prompt, and go one better by adding the format print shops still ask for by name: PDF, and ideally EPS. Right now app.js offers PNG and SVG only, so a user handed a 'send us an EPS or a print-ready PDF' spec has to convert it themselves.

complaints.complaint: Blurry, unscannable print output. 'A blurry QR Code usually happens when someone downloaded a small PNG and stretched it up in the design tool.' The advice is universal and universally ignored: use SVG/PDF/EPS for print, and a 2×2 cm code needs at minimum 300 DPI (236×236 px), ideally 600 DPI (472×472 px).
complaints.source: Multiple category guides including qr-code-generator.com's own 'Blurred QR Code' post and Uniqode's printing guideline; the DPI figures recur across them
complaints.weWinIf: Stop selling PNG by pixel count, which means nothing to anyone. Our size dropdown says '512 px / 1024 px / 2048 px' (index.html around line 1289). Relabel it in physical terms, 'business card, 2 cm at 600 DPI', 'flyer, 4 cm', 'poster, 15 cm', and show the resulting DPI. Then make SVG the primary button and PNG the secondary, with one line of copy: for anything that goes to a printer, send the SVG.

complaints.complaint: Logos and heavy customization silently break the code. The guidance across the category is that a centre logo must stay around 20-25% of the code's width, must sit on a solid background with 2-4 modules of padding, and requires error-correction level H, and that 'heavy customization (large logo overlays, pattern fills) compounds the problem by eating into the QR Code's error correction capacity.' Every generator offers the feature; none of them stop you.
complaints.source: Uniqode 'Why Is Your QR Code Not Working?', Bitly 'QR code not working', and the wider troubleshooting literature
complaints.weWinIf: This is the best differentiator available and it comes from the category's own failure. If we ever add a logo or colour (we currently hardcode #000 on #fff in helpers.js), ship it with a live headroom meter: force EC level H, compute the fraction of modules the logo actually occludes, and show remaining error-correction budget as a number with a hard stop. 'Your logo is covering 19% of the code, 11% of correction left' is a thing no competitor shows, because showing it would discourage the customization that sells their design tier.

complaints.complaint: WiFi QR codes that fail on iPhone. The recurring cause is unescaped special characters: 'if your SSID or password contains characters like ; : , \ " ', they must be escaped using a backslash,' and 'even a stray space can cause inconsistent behavior across scanners.' Separately, iOS scanners have had documented trouble recognising WPA3 networks.
complaints.source: Apple Support Communities threads 'QR Code to join Wifi does not work' (253875748) and 'Unable to join WiFi using QR Code' (250658189); Apple Developer Forums thread 652510 on WPA3; category troubleshooting guides
complaints.weWinIf: We already do the hard part correctly, helpers.js `escapeWifi` backslash-escapes \ ; , : " exactly per the de-facto spec, and it is unit-tested. Two things are missing. The hidden-network flag is dead code: `buildPayload` emits `H:true;` when `f.hidden` is set, but `renderFields()` never renders a checkbox to set it, so a hidden SSID silently produces a code that will not connect. And WPA3 networks need to be addressed in the UI, the security dropdown offers WPA/WPA2, WEP and open only, so a WPA3 router has no honest option. Add the hidden checkbox, and add a line telling WPA3 users what to expect.

complaints.complaint: People no longer trust QR codes at all. The FTC has issued consumer alerts on scammers hiding harmful links in QR codes, including codes in unsolicited packages; the IC3 issued a PSA on the same in July 2025. Roughly 73% of Americans are reported to scan codes without verification and more than 26 million have been sent to malicious sites. The core problem is structural: 'a QR code conceals its destination entirely until after it's scanned.'
complaints.source: consumer.ftc.gov consumer alerts (Jan 2025 'Scam alert: QR code on an unexpected package'); IC3 PSA250731; CNBC coverage, 27 Jul 2025; Security.org quishing explainer
complaints.weWinIf: The person printing the code carries this problem too, their customers hesitate. Two responses, both cheap. Show the maker exactly what a scanner will see, in full, so they can vouch for it. And offer a printable frame that puts the destination in human-readable text beside the code, 'menu.thecorner.cafe' under a SCAN ME label, because a legible destination is the one thing that converts a suspicious stranger into a scan. That is a security feature and a conversion feature at the same time.

complaints.complaint: The redirect domain itself is a trust problem: 'users generally don't trust QR codes that point to a QR generator's redirect domain and prefer QR codes that go straight to their own website.' Dynamic codes route every scan through the vendor's server, and 'QR codes can track the general location of the user based on the IP address of the device used to scan the code', IP addresses being personal data under GDPR.
complaints.source: Category comparison and analytics documentation, including QR Planet's own GDPR help article and Scanova/Pageloot tracking guides
complaints.weWinIf: Name it as a two-sided harm, the vendor meters you, and it logs the stranger who scanned your poster. Our code has no middleman for either party. This is also the line that makes the app defensible for schools, churches, clinics and anyone with a data-protection form to fill in: nothing is logged because there is nothing in the path.

complaints.complaint: Free tiers are counters, not products. Bitly Free: 2 QR codes per month. Flowcode Free: 2 codes, 500 scans. QR TIGER Free: 3 dynamic codes at 500 scans each. Uniqode: 14-day trial, annual billing only. A restaurant numbering twenty tables, a school labelling thirty Chromebooks, or a warehouse tagging shelves hits the wall on the first afternoon.
complaints.source: bitly.com/pages/pricing and flowcode.com/pricing read directly; QR TIGER free-tier limits from secondary comparison sources
complaints.weWinIf: Batch generation, free, is the sharpest wedge we have and it is currently absent entirely, app.js generates exactly one code at a time. Paste a list of lines or a CSV column, get one printable sheet of labelled codes and/or a zip of SVGs. This is the paid tier at four competitors, it is pure client-side arithmetic, and it converts our architecture into a feature they structurally cannot match at zero price.

complaints.complaint: Codes printed too small to scan. The rules are well established, the 10:1 ratio (a code read from 1 m should be about 10 cm wide), a practical floor around 2×2 cm for arm's-length scanning, and add 20-30% for real-world lighting and angles, but the generator never asks how far away the reader will be standing, so the user finds out at the table tent or the shop window.
complaints.source: Uniqode QR sizing guide and the wider category literature; the 10:1 rule and the 2 cm floor recur consistently
complaints.weWinIf: Ask the one question no competitor asks: how far away is the person scanning? Turn the answer into a stated print width in mm and inches, and offer a true-size on-screen preview so the maker can hold their phone up and test at the real dimension before spending money. Then finish the job with actual printable output, our print stylesheet (index.html line 1181) is the generic portfolio one; it hides the chrome but there is no printable card, no table tent, no label sheet, and no `.printonly` block in the markup at all.

complaints.complaint: The content-type wall. Every competitor opens with a grid of twenty types, vCard, SMS, calendar event, location, App Store, PDF, menu, social, and the ones people actually reach for beyond a URL are the contact card and SMS. A digital business card is the single most common paid use case in the category and drives Uniqode's and Flowcode's whole product line.
complaints.source: Competitor product surfaces (QRCode Monkey, QR TIGER, Uniqode, the-qrcode-generator.com) and Uniqode's digital-business-card positioning; not a quoted user review, so treat the ranking as inference rather than evidence
complaints.weWinIf: We ship five types (app.js `TYPES`: url, text, wifi, tel, email). The missing one that matters is vCard/MeCard, a contact card is static by nature, needs no server, and is the case where 'never expires' is most obviously right. SMS and geo are a few lines each. Adding vCard, SMS and calendar-event takes us from 'a toy' to 'covers what people came for' without touching the architecture. Resist the twenty-tile grid; five well-written forms beat twenty stubs.

tableStakes: Free vector download with no account. WE HAVE IT and it is genuinely good, helpers.js qrToSvg emits a single path of module squares with shape-rendering="crispEdges" and a 4-module quiet zone. This is behind Canva Pro and behind a signup at qr-code-generator.com.
High-resolution PNG for print. WE HAVE IT (512/1024/2048 px, app.js dlPng) but it is labelled in pixels, which tells the user nothing about whether it will print at 2 cm.
Error-correction control. WE HAVE IT, the 'Toughness (survives smudges)' select in index.html offers M/Q/H. Better-worded than any competitor's raw 'L/M/Q/H'.
Correct WiFi payload escaping. WE HAVE IT, helpers.js escapeWifi backslash-escapes \ ; , : " and it is covered by test/helpers.test.mjs. Most free clones get this wrong.

Hidden-network support for WiFi. WE DO NOT HAVE IT in the UI. helpers.js buildPayload already emits H:true; when f.hidden is set, but app.js renderFields() never renders a checkbox for it, the code path is unreachable, so hidden SSIDs silently produce a code that will not connect.

A contact-card (vCard/MeCard) type, plus SMS, geo and calendar-event. WE HAVE NONE OF THEM, app.js TYPES contains only url, text, wifi, tel, email. vCard is the category's most common use case after a plain link and the one where 'static forever' is most obviously the correct answer; the other three are a handful of lines each in helpers.js buildPayload.

Logo in the centre, plus colour and transparent-background options. WE HAVE NEITHER. helpers.js draws a bare module grid with colours hardcoded #000000 on #ffffff in both qrToSvg and drawQrToCanvas. Universal at competitors, even the fully free QRCode Monkey does logos and colours, and transparent PNG is a Canva Pro feature we could give away, but logo overlay is also the #1 documented cause of unscannable codes, so the right answer is a constrained version with a visible error-correction headroom readout, not a copy of theirs.
PDF or EPS export for print shops. WE DO NOT HAVE IT, PNG and SVG only. QRCode Monkey gives away all four formats for free.

A saved list of codes you have made, with re-download. WE DO NOT HAVE IT. Nothing persists: app.js holds everything in the in-memory `fields` object, and sws-prefs.js stores only display preferences. A page reload loses the work, which is a strange gap in a portfolio where every other app keeps your data on the device.
Bulk / batch generation from a pasted list or CSV. WE DO NOT HAVE IT AT ALL. It is a paid feature at QR Code Generator Pro, QR TIGER and Uniqode, and it is pure client-side arithmetic for us.
A 'SCAN ME' frame with the destination in readable text. WE DO NOT HAVE IT. Standard at every competitor, and given the FTC quishing alerts it now does double duty as a trust signal.

The portfolio's own trust stamp. WE DO NOT HAVE IT HERE. The .trust component is fully styled in index.html (rules at lines 437-448 and a print override at 1227) but there is no element with class="trust" anywhere in the markup, the promise appears only as hero prose and a grey footer line, which the cross-portfolio brief specifically says people do not believe.
differentiators: Show the exact encoded string. Print the payload verbatim under the preview with a byte count and a plain caption, 'this is the entire contents of the code; nothing else is added.' It turns our central claim from marketing into something the user verifies with their own eyes, it exposes by contrast that a dynamic code contains someone else's domain, and no funded competitor will copy it.

Ask how far away the reader will stand, then answer in millimetres. Take a scanning distance, apply the 10:1 rule with the documented 20-30% real-world margin, and output a print width in mm and inches plus the DPI the chosen PNG will actually achieve at that width. Then offer a true-size on-screen preview so the code can be scan-tested at its real dimension before anyone pays a printer.

Printable output, not just files. A page of WiFi cards for the guest room, a sheet of labels at a stated physical size for boxes and equipment, a table tent, a framed SCAN ME poster with the destination in legible text underneath. This is where a browser tool beats a dashboard, we already have a portfolio print stylesheet to build on, and the WiFi card is the one thing the iPhone's built-in Wi-Fi QR cannot give you.

A local, device-only history with byte-identical re-export. Static codes are permanent; the thing people lose is the file. Keep a list, label, payload, EC level, module count, date, that re-exports the exact same SVG two years later, with JSON export/import so it can be filed alongside the artwork. Directly answers 'They deleted my QR code and there is no way to retrieve it.'

Honest customization with a headroom meter. If we add a logo and colours, ship them with the guardrail the whole category refuses to build: force EC level H, compute the percentage of modules occluded, show remaining error-correction budget as a live number, and hard-stop before the code becomes unreliable. Turn the category's most common failure into our credibility feature.

Free bulk generation. Paste a list of table numbers, asset tags, room names or URLs; get one printable labelled sheet and a zip of SVGs. This is the paid tier at four competitors and costs us nothing but code.

A permanence receipt. A small printable block recording the payload, error-correction level, QR version and module count, and the date, so a reprint in three years reproduces an identical file. It is the physical-world counterpart to 'never expires' and it makes the promise operational rather than rhetorical.

Black on white by default, with the reason stated. Every competitor pushes colour because colour sells the design tier. We should default to maximum-contrast black-on-white, allow colour deliberately, and say in one line that the code is a machine-readable object first, the same restraint logic that makes signature-maker work.

Offline as a demonstration, not a footnote. Real installable PWA, and an explicit invitation to turn off the network and watch it keep working. Against a category built entirely on server round-trips, that is the claim that cannot be copied by a competitor whose business is the redirect.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: The 2026 QR category has converged on a SaaS-marketing look: near-black hero, one hot neon accent (Flowcode's electric blue-green, QR TIGER's orange, Uniqode's violet), a grid of fifteen to twenty content-type tiles, a large rounded preview card on the right with logo/eye-shape/dot-style pickers, and a Download button that turns out to be a signup wall. Reading as dated: skeuomorphic scanner and phone-camera illustrations, 2020-era 'touchless menu' framing, gradient-filled and drop-shadowed QR codes, and stock photography of people pointing phones at posters. Reading as current: grotesk or mono labels, precise numeric readouts (version, module count, capacity used, bytes), restrained neutral surfaces with a single saturated accent, and honest live previews. There is also a novelty tier, AI 'artistic' QR codes generated with diffusion models, which is fashionable, largely unscannable, and correctly ignored. The one immovable convention is the artefact itself: the code is black on white and must stay that way, so all of the app's colour lives in the chrome and none of it touches the code. A design that respects that boundary visibly is already saying something true about the product.
aesthetic.emotionalContext: Three people open this. First, and most important, the burned one: they made a 'free' code somewhere, printed it on 500 flyers or a laminated table tent, and it stopped working. They are angry, they are suspicious of the next free tool, and they are searching the exact words 'QR code that never expires.' They arrive on desktop, mid-workday, and they will decide whether to trust us in about eight seconds, which means the proof, not the claim, has to be visible without scrolling. Second, the small operator about to spend money: a cafe owner, a market stallholder, a church volunteer, a teacher labelling thirty Chromebooks. Their anxiety is not privacy, it is 'will this scan when it comes back from the printer', and the cost of being wrong is physical and already paid for. Third, the casual host making one WiFi card for the guest room on a phone, ninety seconds, no stakes at all. The design must serve the third without slowing them down and the second without leaving them guessing, which argues for a single-screen tool with the physical-size and scan-test affordances present but quiet, never a wizard. Nothing here is emotionally heavy, so the register is not warmth; it is competence. This should feel like a well-made instrument that gives correct answers, and the anger the first visitor arrives with should be met with precision rather than reassurance.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: precise, printerly, unbranded, verifiable, matter-of-fact, permanent, quietly technical

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: Deep vermilion / burnt registration-orange, around hue 22-26 at chroma ~0.15, on a cool paper. Keep the technical (Space Grotesk) voice, the grid texture and r:8, those are already right. Concretely: change skins.mjs 'qr-maker' from { hue: 142, chroma: 0.13 } to roughly { hue: 24, chroma: 0.15 }, paper stays 'cool', and consider a support hue around 210 for the rare secondary accent.
colorRecommendation.rationale: The current setting is the worst adjacency in the portfolio. skins.mjs puts five apps inside a 70-degree arc of green, bracket-maker 104, home-inventory 124, qr-maker 142, grocery-list 158, sub-plans 174, and qr-maker's nearest neighbour, grocery-list at 158, is also cool paper at chroma 0.14, which is within noise of qr-maker's 0.13. Two cool greens sixteen degrees apart at the same chroma and the same value are not two products. On the other side, home-inventory at 124 shares qr-maker's technical voice AND its grid texture, so the only separator there is paper temperature. The green slot cannot be rescued by pushing chroma or value; it needs to leave. The arc between secret-santa (8) and specials-planner (38) is the single largest unoccupied gap on the wheel in this system, and both of its neighbours are warm-paper editorial serif apps at moderate chroma, so a cool-paper, high-chroma, grotesk app at 24 will never be mistaken for either, because it differs on hue, temperature, voice and texture simultaneously. The hue is also right on the merits rather than merely available: vermilion is the colour of printer's registration marks, crop marks and trim guides, and this is a tool whose entire job is producing something that goes to a printer and must come back correct. Warm ink on a cool grey-blue page with a faint module grid reads as a press proof sheet, which is exactly the promise. It also puts maximum distance between the chrome and the artefact, a warm orange interface framing a pure black-and-white code makes the code look like the object and the app look like the workbench, reinforcing the differentiator that we never colour the modules. One caution to design around: high-chroma orange sits close to warning territory, so pull the value deep (accent lightness near 0.52, not a fluorescent safety orange), and make sure the app's own error and warning states, the too-much-data toast in app.js, the error-correction headroom meter if we build it, are distinguished by iconography and border weight rather than by being red, or they will disappear into the brand.
colorRecommendation.avoid: Greens from roughly 100 to 180, that arc already holds five apps and is where qr-maker currently and wrongly sits. Avoid the blue-to-violet band 234-276 (pill-schedule, caregiver-log, team-parent, signature-maker, pdf-tools), which is also where most of the QR category's own branding lives, so it would collide internally and externally at once. Avoid near-achromatic ink, which is signature-maker's whole identity. Avoid neon or fluorescent treatments and dark-hero-with-glow layouts, that is Flowcode's register and it is the aesthetic of the subscription products we are positioned against. Avoid warm cream paper here; it would pull the app toward specials-planner and secret-santa and soften a tool that should read as instrumentation. And most specifically: never apply the accent, or any gradient, to the QR modules themselves, the code stays #000 on #fff, and the fact that we refuse to prettify it is part of the argument.
